fields.title: Ruth
fields.subtitle: Rut, “The Book of Ruth”
fields.description: A short story from the dark days of the judges, told with rare tenderness. Famine drives a family from Bethlehem to Moab, and ten years later Naomi comes home a widow, without her sons, saying “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me home empty.” With her comes her Moabite daughter-in-law, who would not leave her: “Your people are now my people, and your God is now my God.” Then the barley harvest, the field of Boaz, a night on the threshing floor, and a family redeemer at the town gate, until the empty are filled and a baby is born who will be the grandfather of David. A book about faithful love, human and divine, and about God at work in ordinary days. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Ruth about?
qa.answer: A Moabite widow, Ruth, who refuses to leave her Israelite mother-in-law Naomi after both their husbands die, and goes with her to Bethlehem, taking Naomi’s people and God as her own. Gleaning in the harvest fields, she meets Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s husband, who treats her with great kindness and, as family redeemer, marries her and restores the family’s land and name. Their son Obed is the grandfather of King David (4:17). Its four chapters move Naomi from emptiness to fullness, and show God’s care working through ordinary people’s faithfulness.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Ruth, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition assigned it to Samuel. Because its closing genealogy ends with David, it was written no earlier than his time. Some scholars date it to the period of the kings; others to the time after the exile, when its warm welcome of a foreign wife would have spoken into debates about marriage outside Israel. The story itself is set “in the days when the judges judged” (1:1), probably a few generations before David.

qa.question: What is a kinsman-redeemer in Ruth?
qa.answer: A close relative with the right and duty to rescue a family member in trouble: to buy back land a poor relative had been forced to sell (Leviticus 25:25), and, by a related custom (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), to raise up an heir for a man who died childless. This translation calls him a “family redeemer”. In Ruth 4, a nearer relative declines the role for fear of harming his own inheritance, and Boaz takes it on, buying Elimelech’s land and marrying Ruth. Christians have long seen in him a picture of Christ, who redeems his people at his own cost.

qa.question: What does “hesed” mean in the book of Ruth?
qa.answer: Hesed is the Hebrew word for loyal, committed kindness that goes beyond what duty requires; this translation renders it “faithful love”. It appears at three turning points in the book: Naomi’s prayer for her daughters-in-law (1:8), her praise of the LORD when she learns where Ruth has gleaned (2:20), and Boaz’s praise of Ruth on the threshing floor (3:10). Ruth shows it to Naomi, Boaz shows it to Ruth, and behind them both the LORD shows it to all.

qa.question: Why is Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus?
qa.answer: Because she was the great-grandmother of King David, from whose line the Messiah was promised. Matthew’s Gospel names her in its list of Jesus’s ancestors, “Boaz was the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5), alongside Tamar, Rahab and the wife of Uriah. That a Moabite woman, from a people Deuteronomy barred from Israel’s assembly, should be an ancestor of the Messiah has long been read as a sign that God’s promise to bless all the families of the earth was meant for every nation.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
But Ruth said, “Stop pressing me to leave you and turn away from following you. Wherever you travel, I will travel with you; wherever you stop for the night, I will stop as well. Your people are now my people, and your God is now my God.

— Ruth 1:16

The book of Ruth begins with a date that should make a reader wary: “In the days when the judges judged”. Anyone who has just read Judges knows what those days were like. Idols in private shrines, tribes at war with one another, a Levite’s concubine from Bethlehem abused to death in Gibeah. Everyone did what they thought was right.

And then, in the same years and from the same town, comes this. Four short chapters, a story of famine and funerals, of harvest fields and a night on a threshing floor and a meeting of elders at the town gate. There are no battles, no kings, no miracles. There are two widows, a wealthy farmer, and a baby. And by the last verse the story has quietly arrived at the name of Israel’s greatest king.

Ruth is one of the most beautifully told stories in the Bible. It is also one of the most carefully built, and much of its meaning lies in the way it is put together. It rewards slow reading.

From full to empty

The first five verses are a catalogue of loss. A famine drives Elimelech of Bethlehem, whose town’s name means “house of bread”, to Moab with his wife Naomi and their two sons. There Elimelech dies. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then the sons die too, “and the woman was left alone, without her two sons and without her husband.” In a world where a widow’s safety lay in her husband and her sons, Naomi has nothing.

When she hears that “the LORD had come to the help of his people and given them food”, she sets out for home, and urges her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah, weeping, goes. Ruth will not:

The place where you die is where I will die and be buried. May the LORD deal with me ever so severely if anything except death comes between us.”

— Ruth 1:17

With the words just before this, “Your people are now my people, and your God is now my God”, a Moabite widow binds herself to an old woman with nothing to offer, to a foreign people, and to the God of Israel. She calls on the LORD by name. It is a conversion as well as a promise.

The women of Bethlehem scarcely recognise Naomi when she arrives. Her name means “pleasant”, and she will not answer to it: “Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me home empty.” She is not wrong about what has happened to her. But she is wrong about one thing. She has not come home empty. Ruth is standing beside her. And the chapter ends with a quiet note of hope: they arrive “as the barley harvest was beginning.”

“As it happened”

Chapter 2 introduces Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, “a man of wealth and standing”. Ruth goes out to glean, to pick up the grain left behind by the harvesters, which the law of Moses reserved for the poor, the widow and the foreigner. And the narrator says, with a straight face: “As it happened, she came to the part of the field that belonged to Boaz.”

It is a lovely piece of understatement. The book almost never tells us that God is acting. It does so only twice: at the beginning, when the LORD gives his people food, and at the end, when he gives Ruth a son. In between, everything seems to happen by chance, and by the choices of ordinary people. But no reader believes it is chance. Ruth is the Bible’s great story of providence, God working out his purposes through the hidden turns of daily life, through a famine, a field, and a kindness.

Boaz notices Ruth at once. He tells her to stay in his field, orders his young men not to touch her, gives her water and bread and roasted grain, and quietly tells his workers to pull out stalks for her to find. When she asks why a foreigner should find such favour, he answers with a blessing that the rest of the book will answer:

May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you receive your full wages from the LORD, the God of Israel, beneath whose wings you have come for refuge.”

— Ruth 2:12

Ruth comes home with about twenty quarts of barley, far more than any gleaner could expect. And when Naomi hears whose field it was, the bitterness breaks: “The LORD has not stopped showing his faithful love to the living and to the dead.” Then she adds a word that changes the whole story: “He is one of our family redeemers.”

Faithful love

The key word of the book is the Hebrew hesed, translated here “faithful love”. It means the kindness that goes beyond what duty requires, the loyalty that keeps faith with someone when it would be easier to let go. It appears three times, at the three turning points of the story.

  • Naomi prays that the LORD will show her daughters-in-law faithful love, “just as you showed it to the men who died and to me” (1:8).
  • Naomi blesses the LORD, who “has not stopped showing his faithful love to the living and to the dead” (2:20).
  • Boaz tells Ruth that the faithful love she has now shown “is greater than what you showed before” (3:10).

The book is a study of what hesed looks like in human lives. Ruth shows it to Naomi by refusing to leave her. Boaz shows it to Ruth by going far beyond the law. And behind them both, unseen but never absent, the LORD shows it to all of them. The faithful love of God is often carried by the faithful love of his people.

The threshing floor

Chapter 3 is the most delicate scene in the book. Naomi, now planning for Ruth’s future, tells her to wash, dress well, and go down by night to the threshing floor where Boaz is winnowing barley. When he lies down, she is to uncover his feet and lie there, “and he will tell you what you should do.”

It is a bold plan, and readers have long noticed how the scene is charged with possibility. But the book is careful to show that nothing improper happens. When Boaz wakes at midnight to find a woman at his feet, it is Ruth who tells him what to do:

“Who are you?” he asked. She answered, “I am Ruth, your servant. Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant, for you are a family redeemer.”

— Ruth 3:9

The word for “wing” is the same one Boaz had used in the field, when he blessed her for coming to take refuge beneath the LORD’s wings. Ruth is asking Boaz to be the answer to his own prayer. To spread the corner of one’s cloak over a woman was a way of claiming her in marriage, and Boaz understands her at once. He praises her, calls her “a woman of real worth”, and promises to act. But there is a complication: another relative is more closely related, and has the first right.

The family redeemer

To understand chapter 4, it helps to know what a family redeemer was. In Israel’s law, land was not to be lost from a family for ever. If a man fell into poverty and had to sell his land, “the relative closest to him, his redeemer, is to come and buy back what his kinsman sold.” Another law, in Deuteronomy, provided that if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow, and her first son would carry the dead man’s name. Ruth’s story brings the two customs together.

At the town gate, before ten elders, Boaz puts the case to the nearer relative, whom the narrator pointedly does not name: Boaz calls him “Mr. So-and-so”. He is happy to buy Elimelech’s field. But when he hears that the field comes with Ruth, and that her son would inherit it in Mahlon’s name, he backs away: “I would ruin my own inheritance.” He takes off his sandal, the sign of a transfer, and Boaz buys the land and takes Ruth as his wife, “so that the dead man’s name may be kept alive on his inheritance.”

The man who would not risk his inheritance is forgotten; we do not even know his name. The man who took on another family’s loss at his own cost is remembered wherever the Bible is read.

A Moabite in Bethlehem

The book never lets us forget where Ruth came from. She is “Ruth the Moabite” again and again, even after she has made Israel her home. That matters, because Moab was no friendly neighbour. Genesis traces its origin to the incest of Lot’s daughters; Moab had hired Balaam to curse Israel in the wilderness; and Deuteronomy says that “No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD.”

And yet here is a Moabite woman, coming to shelter under the wings of Israel’s God, received by the people of Bethlehem, blessed by the elders in the names of Rachel and Leah, and made the great-grandmother of David. Readers have long seen in her a sign that the promise to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, was never meant to stop at Israel’s borders. Faith, not birth, brings her in.

From empty to full

Ruth bears a son, and the story ends where it began, with Naomi. The women of Bethlehem who had heard her say “the LORD has brought me home empty” now gather around her:

The women said to Naomi, “Praise the LORD, who has not left you this day without a family redeemer! May his name be renowned in Israel.

— Ruth 4:14

They speak of Ruth as one who “loves you and means more to you than seven sons”, and they name the baby in Naomi’s honour: “Naomi has a son!” The woman who went away full and came back empty is full again. And then, in a single sentence, the book opens out: the child is Obed, who “became the father of Jesse, David’s father.”

The short genealogy that closes the book traces the line from Perez, the son of Judah and Tamar, through Boaz, to David. Nothing in the story had pointed to a king. That is the point. While Israel’s leaders were doing what they thought was right, God was preparing a king in a farmhouse in Bethlehem, through a foreign widow’s loyalty and a farmer’s kindness.

How to read Ruth

Read it in one sitting; it takes perhaps twenty minutes. Then read it again, and watch for the echoes: empty and full, the wings, the word “redeem”, the women of Bethlehem at the beginning and the end. Notice how much of the story is told in speech, and how kindly the characters speak to one another. In Jewish practice Ruth is read at the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival Christians know as Pentecost.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition assigned it to Samuel. Since its genealogy ends with David, it was written no earlier than his reign; some scholars place it in the time of the kings, and others after the exile, when its welcome of a foreign wife would have spoken to a sharp debate about marriage outside Israel. Christians hold different views on its date while agreeing on its place among the Scriptures and its link to the story of David.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Ruth are worth knowing before you begin.

“Faithful love.” The Hebrew hesed, rendered in older Bibles “kindness” or “mercy”, is translated “faithful love” throughout the book.

“Family redeemer.” The Hebrew go’el, often rendered “kinsman” or “kinsman-redeemer”, is translated “family redeemer”: the close relative whose duty was to buy back what a family had lost.

Names of God. “The LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name; Naomi also speaks of God as “the Almighty”, the old title Shaddai.

Measures and plain speech. Ancient measures are given in modern terms, so that Ruth’s day of gleaning comes to “about 20 quarts of barley”, and Boaz’s greeting to the nameless relative, an idiom for someone the speaker will not name, becomes “Mr. So-and-so”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Ruth 1
fields.body_html:
Naomi and Ruth come back to Bethlehem

In the days when the judges judged, a famine struck the land. So a man from Bethlehem in Judah set out with his wife and his two sons to live for a while as an outsider in the country of Moab. The man was called Elimelech, his wife was called Naomi, and his two sons were called Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came into the country of Moab and settled there. Then Elimelech, Naomi’s husband, died, leaving her with her two sons. The sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. They lived there for about ten years. Then both Mahlon and Chilion died as well, and the woman was left alone, without her two sons and without her husband. Then she got ready with her daughters-in-law to go back from the country of Moab, because she had heard there that the LORD had come to the help of his people and given them food. She set out from the place where she had been living, with her two daughters-in-law, and they took the road back to the land of Judah. But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go home, both of you, each to the house of your mother. May the LORD show you faithful love, just as you showed it to the men who died and to me. May the LORD grant that each of you finds rest in the home of a new husband.” Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud. They said to her, “No! We will go back with you to your people.” But Naomi said, “Turn back, my daughters. Why go with me? Do I still have sons inside my womb who could become your husbands? Go back, my daughters, go on your way, for I am too old to marry again. Even if I thought there was still hope for me, even if I had a husband tonight and then gave birth to sons, would you then wait until they had grown up? Would you then keep yourselves from marrying? No, my daughters! My lot is far more bitter than yours, for the hand of the LORD has turned against me.” Again they wept aloud. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth held on to her. Naomi said, “See, your sister-in-law has turned back, home to her people and her gods. Follow your sister-in-law back.” But Ruth said, “Stop pressing me to leave you and turn away from following you. Wherever you travel, I will travel with you; wherever you stop for the night, I will stop as well. Your people are now my people, and your God is now my God. The place where you die is where I will die and be buried. May the LORD deal with me ever so severely if anything except death comes between us.” When Naomi saw that Ruth was set on going with her, she said no more to her. So the two of them traveled on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was in an uproar over them, and the women said, “Can this be Naomi?” She said to them, “Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me home empty. Why call me Naomi? The LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has brought disaster on me.” So Naomi came back, and with her came her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabite, who had come back from the country of Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem as the barley harvest was beginning.

fields.title: Ruth 2
fields.body_html:
Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz

Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of wealth and standing from the clan of Elimelech. His name was Boaz. Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go out to the fields and glean ears of grain behind anyone who will look on me with favor.” Naomi answered her, “Go, my daughter.” So she set out, came to a field and gleaned behind the harvesters. As it happened, she came to the part of the field that belonged to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech. Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem. He greeted the harvesters, “The LORD be with you!” and they answered him, “May the LORD bless you!” Boaz asked his servant who was in charge of the harvesters, “Whose young woman is this?” The servant in charge of the harvesters answered, “She is a young Moabite woman, the one who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab. She said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.’ So she came, and she has been on her feet from early morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter.” Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen to me, my daughter. Do not go to glean in any other field, and do not move on from this one. Stay here close to my young women. Keep your eyes on the field they are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have ordered the young men not to lay a hand on you. And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink from the water the young men have drawn.” Ruth fell face down and bowed to the ground. She said to him, “Why have I found such favor with you, that you would take notice of me, when I am a foreigner?” Boaz answered her, “I have heard the whole story of what you have done for your mother-in-law after your husband’s death: how you left your father and mother and the land where you were born, and came to a people you had never known before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you receive your full wages from the LORD, the God of Israel, beneath whose wings you have come for refuge.” She said, “May I go on finding favor in your eyes, my lord. You have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not even one of your servant women.” When mealtime came, Boaz said to her, “Come over here and help yourself to some bread. Dip your piece in the sour wine.” So she sat down beside the harvesters, and he passed her some roasted grain. She ate all she wanted and still had some left over. When she got up to glean, Boaz gave orders to his young men: “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not embarrass her. And even pull out some stalks from the bundles for her and leave them for her to glean. Do not scold her.” So Ruth gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it came to about 20 quarts of barley. She picked it up and went into the town, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gleaned. Ruth also brought out what she had left over after eating her fill, and gave it to her. Her mother-in-law asked her, “Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you!” So Ruth told her mother-in-law about the man she had worked with. “The man I worked with today is named Boaz,” she said. Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May the LORD bless him! The LORD has not stopped showing his faithful love to the living and to the dead.” Naomi went on, “That man is a close relative of ours. He is one of our family redeemers.” Then Ruth the Moabite said, “He even told me, ‘Stay close to my workers until they have finished all my harvest.’” Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, “It is best, my daughter, that you go out with his young women. In someone else’s field you might be harmed.” So Ruth stayed close to Boaz’s young women and gleaned until the barley and wheat harvests were over. And she went on living with her mother-in-law.

fields.title: Ruth 3
fields.body_html:
Ruth at the threshing floor

Naomi, her mother-in-law, said to her, “My daughter, is it not time I looked for a settled home for you, where your life will go well? Now Boaz, whose young women you have been working with, is our relative, is he not? Tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. So bathe, put on perfumed oil, dress yourself well, and go down to the threshing floor. But keep out of the man’s sight until his eating and drinking are over. When he lies down, mark the spot where he is lying. Then go to him, uncover his feet and lie down there, and he will tell you what you should do.” Ruth answered her, “I will do everything you tell me.” So she went down to the threshing floor and did exactly as her mother-in-law had instructed her. Boaz ate and drank and was in a happy mood. He went off and lay down at the far end of the grain pile, and she came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down. In the middle of the night the man woke with a start and turned over. A woman was lying at his feet! “Who are you?” he asked. She answered, “I am Ruth, your servant. Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant, for you are a family redeemer.” He said, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter! This faithful love you have shown now is greater than what you showed before, since you have not looked to the young men for a husband, whether poor or rich. So now, my daughter, have no fear. Whatever you ask, I will do for you. The whole town knows you are a woman of real worth. It is true that I am a family redeemer, but there is a family redeemer more closely related than I am. Stay here for the night. In the morning, if he will act as redeemer for you, well and good: let him do it. But if he does not want to redeem you, then as surely as the LORD lives, I will redeem you myself. Lie down here until morning.” So she lay at his feet until morning, but she got up before it was light enough for anyone to recognize another. And he said, “It must not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor.” Then he said, “Hand me the shawl you have on and hold it out.” When she held it out, he measured six measures of barley into it and set the load on her. Then he went into the town. When she came to her mother-in-law, Naomi said, “How do things stand with you, my daughter?” Then Ruth told her everything the man had done for her. She said, “He gave me these six measures of barley. ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed,’ he told me.” Naomi said, “Stay here quietly, my daughter, until you know how things fall out. The man will not rest until he has brought the matter to an end today.”

fields.title: Ruth 4
fields.body_html:
Boaz acquires the land and marries Ruth

Meanwhile Boaz had gone up to the town gate and taken a seat there. Just then the family redeemer Boaz had spoken about came by. Boaz called to him, “Come over here and sit down, Mr. So-and-so.” So the man came over and sat down. Then Boaz took ten men from the elders of the town and said, “Please sit down here.” And they sat down. Then he said to the family redeemer, “Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is putting up for sale the plot of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. I thought I should tell you about it and say, ‘Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and of the elders of my people.’ If you are willing to redeem it, then do so. If you are not, tell me, so that I know. For no one has the right to redeem it except you, and I come next after you.” “I will redeem it,” he said. Then Boaz said, “On the day you buy the field from Naomi, and from Ruth the Moabite, the dead man’s widow, you acquire Ruth as well, to keep the dead man’s name alive on his inheritance.” The family redeemer replied, “Then I cannot redeem it for myself, or I would ruin my own inheritance. You take over my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it.” In earlier times in Israel, this was how redemption and exchange were made final: one man took off his sandal and gave it to the other. This was how an agreement was witnessed in Israel. So when the family redeemer said to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself,” he took off his sandal. Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “Today you are witnesses that I am acquiring from Naomi everything that belonged to Elimelech and everything that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon. I am also acquiring Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon’s widow, to be my wife, so that the dead man’s name may be kept alive on his inheritance and not be cut off from among his relatives or from the gate of his hometown. Today you are witnesses.” All the people at the gate and the elders answered, “We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman who is coming into your home like Rachel and Leah, the two women who built up the family of Israel. May you thrive in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem. Through the children the LORD gives you by this young woman, may your family be like the family of Perez, the son Tamar bore to Judah.” So Boaz took Ruth home, and she became his wife. He slept with her, and the LORD let her conceive, and she gave birth to a son. The women said to Naomi, “Praise the LORD, who has not left you this day without a family redeemer! May his name be renowned in Israel. He will renew your life and take care of you when you are old. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and means more to you than seven sons, is the one who has given birth to him.” Then Naomi took the child, laid him on her lap, and cared for him. The women who lived nearby gave him a name. “Naomi has a son!” they said, and they called him Obed. He became the father of Jesse, David’s father.

The family line from Perez to David

These are the descendants of Perez. Perez fathered Hezron. Hezron fathered Ram, and Ram fathered Amminadab. Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon. Salmon fathered Boaz, and Boaz fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

— Ruth 4:22

The book of Ruth ends with a list of names, and the last name is David. A story that seemed to be about two widows and their next meal turns out, in its final line, to have been about the throne of Israel all along. The people in it never knew. Ruth probably never saw her great-grandson. Naomi held Obed on her lap and could not have guessed whose grandfather he would be.

The question the book leaves with you

That is the question Ruth leaves with its readers: do you believe God is at work in the ordinary days? The book contains no visions, no prophets, no voice from heaven. It has a famine, a long walk, a day’s work in someone else’s field, a conversation at night, and a meeting at the town gate. Its characters make decisions of loyalty and kindness without knowing where they lead. And through all of it, “as it happened”, God is building a family and preparing a king.

Naomi had decided that “the hand of the LORD has turned against me.” She was grieving, and the book does not scold her for it. But it lets her be proved wrong. The emptiness was real, and it was not the end. The one who seemed to have nothing to give, a foreign daughter-in-law, turned out to be the gift.

Where the story goes next

In the English Bible, Ruth sits between Judges and 1 Samuel, and that is where it belongs in the story. 1 Samuel will tell how Israel got its first king, and then how God chose another, a shepherd boy from Bethlehem, the son of Jesse, the grandson of Obed. Many centuries later, the prophet Micah would say that a ruler was still to come from “Bethlehem Ephrathah, too small to be counted among the clans of Judah”.

The New Testament names Ruth in the very first chapter. Matthew’s list of the ancestors of Jesus includes four women besides Mary, and two of them belong to this very household: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab. Boaz was the father of Obed by Ruth.” A Canaanite and a Moabite, in the line of the Messiah. And the shape of Boaz’s kindness has long been read as a picture of Christ: the near relative who takes on our loss at his own cost, redeems what we could not buy back, and gives a stranger a home and a name. Jesus himself used the image of the wings, lamenting over Jerusalem: “How many times I have wanted to gather your children together, the way a hen draws her chicks under her wings!”

Where to go from here

Ruth is short, but the church has never stopped preaching it, and some of the best of that preaching is in this library:

  • On the whole book. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Ruth: Union with Christ” reads the marriage of Ruth and Boaz as a picture of the union of Christ and the church.
  • On Ruth’s choice (Ruth 1). Jonathan Edwards’s sermon “Ruth’s Resolution”, on Ruth 1:16, in Selected Sermons of Jonathan Edwards.
  • On the field of Boaz (Ruth 2). Hudson Taylor’s A Full Reward, on Boaz’s blessing in Ruth 2:12; and Charles H. Spurgeon’s chapter “Spiritual Gleaning”, on Ruth 2:15, in Talks to the Farmer.
  • On the redeemer (Ruth 3–4). A. B. Simpson’s sermon Our Kinsman Redeemer, which reads Boaz as a picture of Christ.
  • For reading with children. “Ruth Stays with Naomi” and “Boaz the Redeemer” in Tell Me the Story – Book 2: Out of Egypt, an Ochorus Original.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Ruth in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then go back to where it began, to a widow on the road from Moab, with nothing to offer and nowhere certain to go, who chose the people and the God of another woman, and found herself sheltered beneath his wings:

May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you receive your full wages from the LORD, the God of Israel, beneath whose wings you have come for refuge.”

— Ruth 2:12
